Chapter 6: War, Risk, and the Expanding Boundaries of Freedom
Imagine stepping into a world that’s both painfully familiar and completely transformed. That’s what Harriet Tubman faced as the Civil War erupted. Suddenly, the old lines—North and South, freedom and bondage—weren’t just ideas. They’d become real, dangerous battlefields. For someone like Harriet, who’d spent years moving in the shadows, dodging capture, the chaos of war brought fresh dangers—but also brand new opportunities.
Picture this: after a lifetime of hiding, she’s now out in the open. Her unique skills? Suddenly, they’re in high demand. Generals and abolitionists needed someone who truly knew the land—its winding backroads, its secret waterways. And Harriet was that someone. She became a scout, a spy, and, before long, a leader.
There’s this powerful story—one night, the air thick with pine and gunpowder, a group of Union soldiers waited in the dark, hearts pounding. Unsure. Nervous. Harriet was at their side, calm and focused. She led them through the shadows, her quiet confidence guiding the way. All those years trusting her instincts, reading the land and the people around her, led up to this moment. The mission? To free enslaved people along the Combahee River. It was dangerous, no doubt. But for Harriet, the risk was always worth it. And when dawn finally broke, hundreds were free. Their lives—and their futures—forever changed.
Most people don’t realize just how radical it was for a Black woman to command troops, to plan raids, to sit at the table with military leaders and negotiate. It didn’t just shift the boundaries for Harriet—it shifted them for everyone who saw her courage in action. The war was like a crucible, burning away old beliefs and forcing new possibilities into the world.
But with war, there’s always loss. Friends and allies didn’t all make it. Violence was everywhere, and that promise of freedom? Sometimes it was delayed, sometimes even denied. Harriet saw the cost up close—families separated, dreams put on hold. And still, even in those darkest moments, she never let go of the belief that freedom wasn’t just a word. It was a right. Something you fight for, no matter the cost.
The Civil War years changed Harriet’s world, but they also deepened her sense of purpose. She wasn’t just a conductor on the Underground Railroad anymore. She’d become a living symbol—a reminder of what’s possible when ordinary people refuse to accept the world as it is. Those boundaries of freedom? They used to be so narrow you could barely see past them. Now, thanks to Harriet and those who followed her lead, they stretched further than anyone could ever have imagined.
